extracted.intended_audience: general public (patients, teachers, journalists, policymakers) wanting to make sense of science stories and peer review
extracted.subtask_description: A practical guide for non-specialists on how to interpret science reporting and how the peer review process affects the trustworthiness of scientific claims. Focuses on using peer review as an indicator of whether research has been scrutinised and should be taken seriously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review (definition and role)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a system used by scientists to decide which research results should be published in a scientific journal. This system, called peer review, subjects scientific research papers to independent scrutiny by other qualified scientific experts (peers) before they are made public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the presence of peer review to understand that research has been examined by other experts prior to publication; it is the gatekeeping mechanism used to decide what is published in scholarly journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication conveys that research is valid, significant and original
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review can help you make sense of science stories as it tells you that the research has passed the scrutiny of other scientists and is considered valid, significant and original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a study has undergone peer review and been published, it indicates those three qualities (validity, significance, originality). Treat reported research that lacks peer-review backing with greater caution, especially when making health or policy decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific statements are distinct from other claims because of peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review means that statements made by scientists in scientific journals are critically different from other kinds of statements or claims, such as those made by politicians, newspaper columnists or campaign groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the distinction to give greater weight to scientific journal statements (when peer-reviewed) compared with unvetted claims; recognise that peer review makes science more than just another opinion, though it does not make it infallible.
